name: 660 BC Solar Particle Event

phenomena.details: Sharp Delta-14C rise of ~10 per mil over 3-4 years in tree rings, corroborated by 10Be and 36Cl in Greenland ice cores - a hard-spectrum solar proton event.
Hard energy spectrum inferred: F(>30 MeV) = 2.09 (+/-0.75) x 10^10 cm^-2 and F(>200 MeV) = 6.3 x 10^9 cm^-2 (O'Hare et al. 2019).

impacts.description: Extreme solar proton fluence with a hard energy spectrum, depositing ionising radiation into the atmosphere and driving cosmogenic isotope production worldwide.
No contemporary written records linked to the event; identified entirely from cosmogenic isotopes in tree rings and ice cores.

papers.title: Multiradionuclide evidence for an extreme solar proton event around 2,610 B.P. (~660 BC)
papers.authors: O'Hare, P., Mekhaldi, F., Adolphi, F., et al.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.keyFinding: Confirmed the event in 14C, 10Be and 36Cl, deriving a hard-spectrum proton fluence comparable to (about 26% below, within uncertainty) the AD 774/775 event.

papers.title: Relationship between solar activity and Delta-14C peaks in AD 775, AD 994, and 660 BC
papers.authors: Park, J., Southon, J., Fahrni, S., Creasman, P. P., Mewaldt, R.
papers.keyFinding: First identified the ~660 BC radiocarbon peak in German oak and Californian sequoia, with a 3-4 year rise.

papers.title: Multiproxy reconstructions of integral energy spectra for extreme solar particle events of 7176 BCE, 660 BCE, 775 CE, and 994 CE
papers.authors: Koldobskiy, S., Mekhaldi, F., Kovaltsov, G., Usoskin, I.
papers.journal: Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics
papers.keyFinding: Reconstructed the integral energy spectrum of the 660 BC event alongside the other major extreme SPEs.

summary: A hard-spectrum extreme solar proton event around 664-663 BC, confirmed independently by radiocarbon in tree rings and by 10Be and 36Cl in ice cores, with a fluence comparable to the AD 774 event.
description: First identified as a radiocarbon peak around 660 BC (Park et al. 2017) and later confirmed as a genuine solar proton event by O'Hare et al. (2019) using sub-annual 10Be from the NGRIP ice core together with GRIP 10Be and 36Cl records, this is one of the firmly established pre-instrumental extreme solar particle events. Sakurai et al. (2020) refined its timing to between 664 and 663 BCE. The inferred integral proton fluences, F(>30 MeV) = 2.09 (+/-0.75) x 10^10 cm^-2 and F(>200 MeV) = 6.3 x 10^9 cm^-2, indicate an unusually hard spectrum and a total fluence comparable to (roughly 26% smaller than, but consistent within uncertainty with) the AD 774/775 event, and about an order of magnitude larger than the strongest event of the instrumental era. The 3-4 year rise in radiocarbon has prompted suggestions that the signal may represent one exceptional event or a short cluster of energetic events.
